Grisamine: Grisamine is an antibiotic produced by a strain of streptomyces similar to S. griseoflavus (Sawazaki et al., 1955). It was obtained in the form of needle crystals melted at 167°C to 170°C having C20H30O7 as its empirical formula. Grisamine inhibited the growth of BCG and virulent tubercle bacilli at the concentration of 5 μg per cc in Kirchner liquid medium. Intravenous injection of 160 mg per kg caused the death of mice within one week, but 150 mg per kg was tolerated. Miyamoto and others (1955) conducted mice protection test against experimental tuberculosis with this antibiotic. Thirty mice of an inbred strain were infected with 0.001 mg of virulent tubercle bacilli (H2 strain). Grisamine administration to 10 of them was initiated one day after infection with 30 mg daily dose, and continued for 3 weeks. The effect was evaluated by viable bacterial unit count of the lung, liver and spleen, comparing with other two groups of 10 each. One group had been treated with streptomycin and another group had been left untreated. The result indicated that grisamine has no effect on mouse inoculation tuberculosis.

Homomycin: Homomycin was first isolated by Sumiki and his co-workers (1955) from the culture liquid of a new streptomyces named S. noboritensis. This antibiotic was reported to have a high activity specifically against H37Rv tubercle bacilli and BCG. In addition, it was proved that homomycin has almost no acute toxicity, LD50 being more than 2,000 mg per kg of mouse body weight by intravenous injection. These informations led Yanagisawa and others (1956) to an attempt to confirm the effect of homomycin in vitro and to extend the observation on mice experimental tuberculosis. The result was that homomycin inhibited the growth of H37Rv strain and its variant substrains resistant to streptomycin and isoniazid in Kirchner liquid medium at 1 μg per cc or less than that, but it failed to prolong significantly survival time of heavily infected tuberculous mice.
